title: Fever after chemotherapy (telephone) — recognise, explain and intervene safely

blocks.text: Fever after chemotherapy (telephone) — recognise, explain and intervene safely

Round 5 · Station 2, acute consultation · 20 minutes · Assessed skills A–G according to consultation task; communication (C), clinical judgement (E), concerns (F), welfare (G) particularly tested · Source review: 14 October 2026 · Educational, not an official PACES marking scheme.

You are the medical registrar taking a call from a 55-year-old seven days after cytotoxic chemotherapy. Their temperature is 38.3°C, with chills. Advise them by telephone and arrange safe assessment. Take a focused history, address immediate risks and explain the next steps to the patient or caller.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count. Examiner trap: Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home.

rows: “First I need to check how unwell you are.”
Identify instability and initiate emergency support.
“I will ask targeted questions to guide the next step.”
Recent chemotherapy, new fever and rigors; neutrophil count is not yet available. Ask about breathlessness, collapse, confusion, rigors, catheter and sepsis risks.
“There is a potentially serious cause we must assess.”
Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count.
“I will tell you what happens next and why.”
Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated.

blocks.text: Anxious caller at home; initially thinks paracetamol and sleep might suffice. If asked: no allergy known; lives 30 minutes away, has a family member to drive, and no recent blood count. Respond emotionally to an empathetic explanation; do not volunteer extra clinical signs unless asked.
Q5. What about a central line? MODEL: Assess its infection risk and obtain cultures as clinically feasible, but do not automatically remove it in initial empiric management.
Q4. What if they feel faint? MODEL: Call 999, pre-alert the emergency team, do not ask them to drive.
Q3. What first-line antibiotic? MODEL: NICE CG151 recommends piperacillin–tazobactam monotherapy as initial empirical antibiotic unless patient-specific/local microbiological contraindication.
Q2. Can this wait for blood results? MODEL: No. Organise emergency assessment and prompt empiric antibiotics; collect investigations without undue treatment delay.
Q1. Why is urgent assessment necessary? MODEL: Chemotherapy-associated fever may be neutropenic sepsis even without the current neutrophil count.

FAIL — PATIENT: “I am worried.” CANDIDATE: “It can wait until tomorrow.” [R1 Fail; R7 Fail] EXAMINER: “Which risks did you consider?” CANDIDATE: “None particularly.” [R2/R3 Fail] PATIENT: “What tests will you do?” CANDIDATE: “We will see.” [R4–R6 Fail] Examiner note: misses acute safety and specific clinical actions.

PASS — CANDIDATE: “I am concerned by what you have told me; I need to assess your immediate safety.” [R1 Pass] PATIENT: “What is happening?” CANDIDATE: “Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count.” [R2 Pass; R3 Pass] EXAMINER: “What is your plan?” CANDIDATE: “Immediate emergency attendance by agreed transport or ambulance if unwell; hospital ABCDE, FBC, cultures, lactate, renal function and source assessment without delaying therapy. Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated.” [R4 Pass; R5 Pass] PATIENT: “Is there a risk in waiting?” CANDIDATE: “Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home. I will check you understand the next step.” [R6 Pass; R7 Pass] Examiner note: adequate safe consultation; identify actual time-critical actions.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “Before anything else, are you faint, struggling to breathe or unable to stay alert? I will ensure the right urgent help is here.” [R1 High-performance] PATIENT: “Why the urgency?” CANDIDATE: “Your symptoms can indicate Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count. I need to clarify onset and severity and ensure we do not overlook other acute causes.” [R2 High-performance; R3 High-performance] EXAMINER: “Which steps take priority?” CANDIDATE: “Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home. Investigations: Immediate emergency attendance by agreed transport or ambulance if unwell; hospital ABCDE, FBC, cultures, lactate, renal function and source assessment without delaying therapy. Treatment: Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance; R7 High-performance] PATIENT: “I am frightened.” CANDIDATE: “That is understandable. Which concern would you like me to address first? I will explain the plan, check what you understood and arrange a clear handover.” [R6 High-performance] Examiner note: priority-led, patient-centred, not a script to memorise verbatim.
R2/R3: Failure to identify Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count.

R4: Testing without considering urgency or risks — Immediate emergency attendance by agreed transport or ambulance if unwell; hospital ABCDE, FBC, cultures, lactate, renal function and source assessment without delaying therapy.
R5/R7: Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home.
R6: Overconfident reassurance before explaining uncertainty and immediate plan.
“I need to reassess the immediate risk and act before completing every question.”

“The most important next step is: Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated.”
“I will explain the expected process and confirm the handover.”

Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count. Immediate emergency attendance by agreed transport or ambulance if unwell; hospital ABCDE, FBC, cultures, lactate, renal function and source assessment without delaying therapy. Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated. Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home.

THINK: Suspected neutropenic sepsis: a time-critical cancer-treatment complication even without a known neutrophil count. SAY: clear urgency without alarmism. DO: Alert acute oncology/emergency team; begin empiric IV antibiotics immediately following local neutropenic sepsis protocol, with allergy assessment; resuscitate as indicated. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter; follow current clinical time limits. TRAP: Do not advise waiting for a blood count or for fever to persist; do not manage with antipyretics at home. FINISH: document and hand over to receiving clinician.
